newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Competition to trim SingTel profit growth.
newsitem.headline: Competition to trim SingTel profit growth.

text.p: It may take time, but the end of Singapore Telecommunications Ltd's domestic monopoly will eventually erode its profit margins, analysts said on Wednesday.
"You don't have to be a rocket scientist to see competition is going to affect SingTel's bottom line," said John Chessher, regional telecommunications analyst at Schroders in Bangkok.

Most analysts expect SingTel to report a 13 percent rise in net profit to around S$1.68 billion (US$1.17 billion) in its financial year to March 31, 1997, but say pressure from competition will push this growth down to 11 percent next year. SingTel has enjoyed a monopoly of telecommunications services in Singapore since it was privatised in 1992.
But on April 1, it faces one new competitor, MobileOne (M1), in the mobile phone market and three new rival pager services.
MobileOne is a joint venture of Britain's Cable & Wireless, Hong Kong Telecommunications, Keppel Telecom and Singapore Press Holdings.
The mobile phone market accounted for 17 percent of SingTel's total revenue in its latest half-year to September 30, 1996, and was the fastest expanding source of income.
Analysts say the mobile market is now worth at least S$800 million a year and that they expect to see rapid growth.

The opening of the cellular market is the first stage of a liberalisation of Singapore's telecommunications sector that will eventually see full competition for all basic telephone services from April 2000.

British Telecommunications Plc, the MobileOne consortium partners, and several other local companies have said they will submit bids for the one or two basic telephone service licences when the tenders open formally later this year.
U.S. giant AT&T has also expressed an interest.
Competition there will help erode margins for international direct dialing (IDD) services which currently account for almost half SingTel's income.
Analysts say Singapore's average IDD collection rates have fallen by around 20 percent over the last two years to S$1.86 per minute and see this trend accelerating with competition.
"In the last year alone, IDD call minutes have risen by 14 percent but IDD rates have fallen by the almost exactly same rate," said a local analyst.

Chessher said MobileOne's challenge to SingTel's mobile market would take time to gather pace but would take off after Singapore Communications Minister Mah Bow Tan allows one or two more mobile phone companies to operate from April 2000.
"The duopoly could start cosily," he said. "M1 won't want to rock the boat at first. But by 1999 it will be under pressure to establish itself and the gloves will come off in 2000."
In the S$200 million a year Singapore pager market, one of the new competitors, Hutchison Paging, is targetting SingTel customers with subsidies to persuade them to switch services.
Hutchison is a joint venture of Hutchison Whampoa Ltd, Intraco Ltd and Teledata. The other new paging firms are MobileOne and ST Messaging.
Hutchison aims for 200,000 pager-users in two or three years time, equivalent to 20 percent of the existing one million subscribers. It says 60,000 of these could be SingTel users.
The hope for SingTel shareholders must be that the company can diversify out of its core domestic market, said Mano Sabnani, head of research at DBS Securities.
"While domestic growth rates slow due to competition, contributions from overseas investments will gradually improve," he said. "But the bottom line may still see slower growth."
